episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling.

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down 🔓 [Williams Lake Tribune] Repatriated Tsilhqot’in baskets arrive in Williams Lake from Brooklyn Museum and 🔓 [Williams Lake Tribune] Pear Lake wildfire near Clinton grows to 115,438 hectares, plus 1 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: How can local cultural institutions verify authenticity and prevent AI-generated or fraudulent content from being presented as genuine human-made cultural work? Topics include: Music industry response to AI-generated content (label chart rules, Spotify removal rates, Deezer tagging), Technological distinction between revealing existing work (multispectral imaging of palimpsests) versus manufacturing fake content (generative AI imagery), Institutional capacity gaps in small regional museums and galleries versus large platforms, Tŝilhqot'in basket repatriation from Brooklyn Museum as a case study in provenance documentation and institutional authority, Practical implementation of provenance requirements as a preventive governance measure.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Central Cariboo Arts & Culture Society

discussion.central_question: How can local cultural institutions verify authenticity and prevent AI-generated or fraudulent content from being presented as genuine human-made cultural work?
discussion.riley_position: Local institutions can adopt simple, low-cost practical solutions like provenance documentation requirements and basic imaging technology (infrared photography) without waiting for sophisticated detection infrastructure; the distinction between revealing real work and manufacturing fake work is what matters most.
riley_key_evidence: The Archimedes Palimpsest recovery used multispectral imaging to reveal real human work that had been buried, contrasting with Google's fake satellite imagery generation
Multispectral/infrared imaging tools now cost only a few hundred dollars, making them financially accessible to small organizations
A simple one-page provenance submission requirement can be implemented immediately by any local gallery or archive without new infrastructure
discussion.casey_position: The capacity gap for small institutions is insurmountable without dedicated resources; cheap tools don't guarantee adoption when nobody has the hours to learn and use them properly, and provenance documentation alone doesn't prevent fakes from reaching audiences first.
casey_key_evidence: Spotify removed 75 million fraudulent AI-generated tracks after they already reached the platform, showing detection after-the-fact doesn't prevent harm
Small galleries like the Museum of the Cariboo Chilcotin don't have trust-and-safety teams or detection pipelines like streaming platforms do
The baskets' successful repatriation depended on institutional weight and international standing, not technology—most visual heritage lacks that infrastructure
discussion.resolution: They converged on a practical, implementable compromise: a simple one-page provenance policy for local arts organizations requiring donors to document origin and attribution, combining Casey's recognition of institutional limitations with Riley's low-cost, immediately actionable approach. Neither conceded their larger point but agreed this specific measure was achievable without waiting for external systems.
